newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic may bend to protests after long confusion.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic may bend to protests after long confusion.

text.p: President Slobodan Milosevic's reluctance to provide clear direction has confused and prolonged Serbia's political crisis, but signs grew on Tuesday that he would slowly retreat before opposition protesters.
"In a country where the rule of law doesn't count for much, only the man at the top can enforce a decision on the way ahead and he has not played his cards in public yet," one Western diplomat said.

Milosevic's silence has blunted the impact of initial concessions to an opposition bloc that has protested in the streets for more than eight weeks over the annulment of Serbia-wide municipal elections lost by his Socialist Party (SPS).
A subsequent inquiry by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) confirmed the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition had won 14 of Serbia's 18 biggest towns.

OSCE findings backed SPS authorities into a corner and precipitated an uncoordinated scramble by various state bodies to defuse the pressure without giving away the store in the absence of Milosevic's explicit approval.
Serbia's second largest city Nis has typified the chaos.
A Justice Ministry inquiry last month found Zajedno had been robbed of victory in Nis and ordered the outcome restored.
Hardline local SPS party boss Mile Ilic, in an act of spite designed to sabotage the ruling, withheld four seats from Zajedno and the opposition kept protesting as a result, political sources said.
On Tuesday, the local electoral commission weighed in and restored Zajedno's victory in full.

A few hours later the state-run Tanjug news agency announced that Ilic had been booted out of the SPS. But perhaps to mollify hardliners, the Belgrade SPS mayor Nebojsa Covic, who had backed Zajedno demands, was also expelled.

In another important turnabout on Tuesday, electoral commissioners ruled Zajedno had won the Belgrade city assembly. But the local commission noted the results were preliminary. This left room for appeals, reversals or other delays.

"Because of our bad experiences with the SPS we do not trust them and will continue demonstrating until verification of the very last mandate in ... Belgrade and in all other towns in Serbia," said Slobodan Vuksanovic, spokesman for Zajedno.
Calls by two deputy Serbian prime ministers and the SPS mayor of Belgrade last weekend for "the will of the people to be fully respected" have not been fully answered yet.
Throughout, Milosevic has remained conspicuously silent.
Analysts say he has temporised while authoritarian diehards and democratically-inclined moderates in his coterie have argued over a solution at several emergency meetings.
While they wrangled, Milosevic has brooded over his two options, neither pleasing.

He could concede to the sort of democratic groundswell that eventually voted out other leftist oligarchies in Eastern Europe, or resort to police force and risk ostracism by the West and Economic collapse, if not a Romanian-style bloodbath.

Mindful of the parlous economy in Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia and uncertain about the loyalty of his police if ordered to crush peaceful protests, Milosevic chose on Friday to concede quietly, senior political sources say.
But he appeared to be still searching for ways to do so indirectly, without losing face, in his macho Balkan culture.
"It is the mother of all confusions. Decisions are being made and changed on a daily basis and no one really knows what to do (now)," a senior political source said on Monday.
